title: Trophy Design National Soccer League
text:
Award winning design of the official trophy for the Liga Promerica in Costa Rica, outshining over 800 proposals. This project allowed me to combine my passion for design and sports, celebrating the excellence of Costa Rican football. The trophy symbolizes dedication, teamwork, and the spirit of competition.

In collaboration with the Federation of Football Unafut and the official sponsor Bank Promerica, the design was officially revealed at a high-profile event with extensive media coverage across television, radio, social media, and newspapers.

title: Curio
text:
Curio is a magnifying glass with three magnetic lenses that lets children use AI by pointing at things, not typing. A two-week build at CIID.

Curio was born from the idea of giving children a tool that helps them navigate and explore the world with the support of artificial intelligence, without relying on the often overwhelming experience of smartphones or traditional chatbots.

Using an Arduino Q and a range of electronic components — including an HD camera and an amplified speaker — the team developed a sophisticated yet approachable artefact designed to be intuitive, tangible, and engaging for users of all ages. The device encourages active exploration rather than passive screen consumption, supporting learning through direct interaction with the physical environment.

The true strength of Curio lies in its interchangeable magnetic lenses. Each lens represents a different “personality” or perspective through which users can choose to observe and interpret the world. These lenses function as contextual filters for the prompt sent to the AI agent. For example, by attaching the History lens (orange) and capturing an image using the device’s physical button, the system sends the photo along with instructions to provide simple, child-friendly historical insights about the object being observed. In this way, even very young users can access meaningful explanations and discover new knowledge in an accessible format.

Three lenses were developed for this prototype, and designing the magnetic recognition system that allows the device to identify which lens is attached proved to be a significant technical challenge. The tactile action of removing and changing lenses becomes the way users directly control the prompt being sent to the AI, making interaction with the system physical, intuitive, and immediate.

Over the course of two intensive weeks, the team worked through the full lifecycle of a complex hardware-interaction project, building five successive prototypes before arriving at the final version. This process enabled them to fully experience experimentation, iteration, and progressive refinement.

Through this journey, the team learned how to optimise time, distribute responsibilities effectively, and approach unfamiliar technological challenges with confidence, ultimately achieving the rewarding milestone of delivering a fully functional prototype.

title: PlayStation Reactive Facade
text:
For PlayStation’s headquarters in San Jose, California, I was tasked with designing a custom perforated metal panel featuring iconic PlayStation symbols. This installation is applied to the facade of the reception elevator lobby, adding a distinct visual identity to the space.

My role involved creating a perforated pattern with these symbols, ensuring it integrated seamlessly with the building’s architecture. We also developed additional installations, including video mapping content, a wall installation of PlayStation controllers, and an infinite mirror installation.

The most challenging aspect of the project was visualizing the panel with color lighting behind it. We iterated through various options and utilized parametric patterns to achieve the desired effect. This project reflects a perfect blend of functionality, aesthetics, and brand identity, creating a striking first impression for visitors to PlayStation’s headquarters.

title: Carrie
text: A voice companion robot that holds the daily rhythm of elder care, so families can focus on what matters most. Carrie is a voice activated companion device designed for seniors in home care. It bridges the gap between professional medical visits, supporting both seniors and families during the hours when no other help is present. It is a reminder scheduling system, medication check-ins, and daily conversation all through an ambient expressive face. A caregiver can access a web panel that gives the family real-time visibility into the status of reminders and daily updates.

title: Coral Reef
text:
Making a Touchable Experience is an interactive digital project that translates the abstract issue of coral reef bleaching into a tangible, sensory encounter. Developed as part of an introduction to programming, the project uses Processing to visualise the gradual degradation of a coral reef ecosystem through touch-based interaction.

The experience works by allowing the user to touch the screen, triggering a visible bleaching effect across the coral reef. With each interaction, the colours fade and the reef loses its vitality, mirroring the real-world process of coral bleaching. This interaction is designed as a metaphor for the ecological tipping point faced by coral reefs, where continued stress leads to irreversible damage.

The project is aimed at a general audience, particularly those who may be unfamiliar with climate science or the urgency of coral reef decline. By making the issue interactive rather than purely informational, the project encourages users to engage emotionally as well as intellectually with the problem.

The main learning from this project was how code can be used as a storytelling tool to represent complex global problems. Through this process, the team learned how programming can move beyond technical functionality to communicate meaning, evoke empathy, and create awareness around environmental issues.

title: The Wall
text:
Developed as part of a brief to design a space for unexpected interaction with AI, the installation transforms a passage between classrooms into a responsive environment. Rather than treating the corridor as a neutral in-between, the space reacts to presence, movement, and gesture, turning transition into experience.

Using TouchDesigner and AI-based inputs, three distinct visualisations respond to people and their hands. Vertical light strips activate as visitors move through the space, creating the impression of an AI entity embedded within the room—one that mirrors, mimics, and quietly follows human motion. The visuals rely on lines and particle-based abstractions, playing with the idea of how AI might perceive us through patterns, motion, and data rather than recognizable human forms.

Interaction remains intentionally discreet. There are no instructions or interfaces. AI reveals itself only through movement and gesture, encouraging discovery instead of performance.

The project draws on principles of postphenomenology to explore how AI can exist as a background presence rather than a focal object, shaping experience without demanding attention. In doing so, it reframes AI not as a tool or character, but as an ambient participant in shared space.

title: LDA Stadium Interactive
text:
I had the opportunity to participate in the design of the new stadium for Liga Deportiva Alajuelense, known as the new cathedral of football. This project represents the vision of a future-focused stadium, designed to accommodate 25,000 fans and serve as the heart of a unique sports city easily accessible and vibrant for all ages.

As a parametric architecture landmark, this stadium will be the first of its kind in Central America, setting a new standard for design and functionality. The future of the stadium extends beyond its physical structure; it includes an extensive platform of virtual and real-world experiences that connect fans with players, coaches, and the club.

I was responsible for all renderings and the conceptualization of new interactive installations. The future of the project includes a digital LED facade and integrated lighting and content installations inside the stadium, creating an immersive experience for fans worldwide. This is a project that embodies the passion and community spirit of the Liga Deportiva Alajuelense, bridging the gap between tradition and modernity.

title: Binary Mission
text:
Created with Haley Rowland at CIID, Binary Mission turns binary numbers into a hands-on space adventure for children. Players operate a mission-control panel to guide an alien to the right planet.

A button reveals a destination number on an LED screen. Three black-and-white knobs represent binary digits, while an OLED display shows their decimal equivalent. Players experiment with the knobs, then send their answer. A correct code moves the alien to its destination, where it celebrates with a dance.

The prototype combines an Arduino, LED and OLED displays, a servo motor, and light-dependent resistors. Light reflected from each knob lets the system distinguish its black and white positions and interpret the resulting binary number.

The project introduced the team to these components and highlighted the value of quick, low-fidelity prototypes. Working with physical sensors and moving parts revealed unexpected variables that had to be tested and refined throughout the design process.

title: SpeakAR
text:
Created with Daniela Gómez and Nikhil Sajjan at CIID, SpeakAR explores how immersive technology can support learning that carries into everyday life. The concept focuses on public speaking, giving people a virtual environment in which to practise and build confidence.

The project began by questioning the boundary between physical and digital experiences. Although technology shapes daily life, much of our learning and personal growth happens beyond screens. SpeakAR asks how this ongoing learning might be recognised and rewarded as useful skills.

Built with Meta Quest and Unity, the prototype offers a public-speaking training environment with feedback on vocal tone and speaking pace. Consistent practice is intended to translate into tangible benefits while preparing users for real conversations and presentations.

Rather than replacing face-to-face interaction, the immersive experience acts as a bridge to it. Future iterations could explore feedback on posture and body movement alongside the existing vocal feedback.
